item.title: Stronger rescue efforts in Xizang urged
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Stronger rescue efforts in Xizang urged Xi sends message of condolence to Nepal over mudslide Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, chaired a Party leadership meeting on Friday to deliberate and make arrangements to strengthen rescue and relief efforts in the Xizang autonomous region, where the Gyirong land port along the China-Nepal border and its surrounding areas were hit by a catastrophic mudslide on Wednesday morning. At the start of the meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Xi, who is also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, and other leaders observed a moment of silence to mourn the victims of the disaster. As of press time on Friday, five people were confirmed dead and more than 500 still missing in Gyirong county in Xizang's Shigatse. Nepal has reported 579 deaths, while more than 1,900 people are missing there. On Friday, Xi sent a message of condolence to Nepal's President Ram Chandra Poudel over the mudslide, which was triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse. On behalf of the Chinese government and people, Xi expressed deep condolences for the deceased and offered sincere sympathies to the bereaved families, the injured and the people in the disaster-stricken areas. During the Political Bureau meeting, it was noted that emergency rescue operations in Gyirong county in Xizang's Shigatse have so far been carried out in a swift, orderly and well-coordinated manner under the strong leadership of the CPC Central Committee, with comprehensive efforts underway for the resettlement of affected people and for proper handling of the aftermath. The disaster occurred in a severely cold plateau region with steep valleys, variable weather and many surrounding glaciers and glacial lakes, and potential geological hazards are posing significant challenges to emergency rescue operations, the meeting said. It was emphasized that all relevant authorities and departments should take resolute and effective measures for rescue-related work, search and rescue plans should be formulated in a scientific manner, and every effort should be made to search for and rescue all missing Chinese and foreign nationals. The Party leadership also underlined the need to strengthen multi-department joint consultations, enhance monitoring and early-warning systems, and closely track the stability of the barrier lake and surrounding mountains to effectively prevent secondary disasters. It is essential to reinforce the management of on-site personnel to ensure safety throughout the rescue process, the meeting said, urging proper arrangements for the affected people and meticulous attention to post-disaster relief and support. China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit areas in neighboring Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation, the Party leadership decided. The importance of balancing development and security, preparing for the extreme and worst-case scenarios, and bearing a strong sense of political responsibility and constant vigilance to ensure security and stability in all aspects of work was emphasized at the meeting. Meanwhile, Xi, in his condolence message to Poudel, noted that China and Nepal are connected by mountains and rivers and share a common destiny. China is willing to actively aid Nepal in its rescue efforts and provide support and assistance to the best of its capability, he said. Xi expressed his belief that the people of both countries will be able to work together to prevail over the disaster and rebuild their homes as soon as possible. Premier Li Qiang also sent a message of condolence to Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah. Entrusted by Xi, the Chinese premier traveled to Gyirong county on Thursday to guide rescue and emergency response efforts. While assessing the ground situation and meeting with rescue teams, Li emphasized the need to put the people and their lives above all else and spare no effort in carrying out rescue operations and emergency response work. He said that as long as there is a glimmer of hope, every effort should be made to search for and rescue still those missing. Li later visited temporary shelters for affected residents and conveyed President Xi's concern and care to them. The premier emphasized the need to continue dispatching and transporting disaster-relief supplies and ensure the basic living needs of evacuated and relocated residents. Li heard reports from local authorities and relevant departments about the disaster, and discussed further efforts in rescue and emergency response measures. He highlighted the need to coordinate the deployment of rescue forces and equipment, strengthen on-site unified command and thoroughly ascertain the status of missing persons to conduct effective rescues. Transparency in the release of information regarding the disaster and rescue operations is crucial, he added. caodesheng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Services trade to benefit from policy tailwinds
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Services trade to benefit from policy tailwinds China's trade in services, underpinned by robust growth in knowledge-intensive service-sector exports and burgeoning inbound tourism, is set to benefit from further policy and market developments in the second half, officials and experts said, pointing to the sector's emergence as a key engine of foreign trade growth. Their remarks came ahead of the five-day 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, which is scheduled to open in Beijing on Sept 9, as the country doubles down on efforts to broaden access to its vast services market amid rising protectionist barriers and heightened economic uncertainty. "This year's fair will bring together some 90 countries and international organizations, with more than 1,800 companies set to exhibit on-site," said Yan Dong, vice-minister of commerce, at a news conference on Friday. More than 90 companies and institutions will unveil new technologies, products and services spanning information and communications technology, fintech and digital healthcare, some of which will be making their global debuts or their first showings in China, Yan said. In order to strengthen the competitive edge of Chinese services in global markets, this year's fair will, for the first time, feature a promotion and roadshow area dedicated to overseas expansion services, said Tang Wenhong, vice-mayor of Beijing. China's two-way trade in services posted solid growth in the first half, with total imports and exports rising 8.3 percent year-on-year to 3.8 trillion yuan ($560.4 billion), the Ministry of Commerce said. Services exports surged 17.6 percent, providing a strong boost to foreign trade growth. Notably, knowledge-intensive services exports rose 12.8 percent to 805.67 billion yuan, accounting for 53.5 percent of the total. "With knowledge-intensive services now accounting for more than half of the total, China's services exports have reached an inflection point and are moving further up the value chain," said Bai Wenxi, vice-chairman of the China Enterprise Capital Union, adding that digital technology and artificial intelligence are accelerating the shift, with digital services emerging as a new growth engine. The sector is also set to receive further policy support in the July-December period, as national demonstration zones for the innovative development of trade in services and other measures begin to deliver results, said Yan, adding, "China's trade in services is expected to remain on a positive trajectory this year, with services exports continuing to grow strongly." Wang Peng, a researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said China's expanding services sector is also creating new opportunities for foreign companies, given the country's vast market and well-developed industrial ecosystem. "Foreign companies can leverage their expertise to play a greater role in China's expanding services market and benefit as consumer spending shifts toward higher-quality services," Wang said. Falkor AS, a Norway-based industrial intelligence provider serving the global energy sector, will make its fifth appearance at CIFTIS this year, showcasing its solutions, real-world applications and the results of its work with industry partners, said Wu Haifeng, Falkor's senior vice-president. Norway will be the guest country of honor at this year's fair. Norwegian businesses hope to use the occasion to build new partnerships in China, said Wu, who is also vice-chairman of the Norwegian Business Association China. "Over the next five years, we will continue to increase our investment in China, deepen local partnerships and use industrial intelligence to boost operational performance and advance the green transition of the energy sector," Wu said. Beijing, this year's host of CIFTIS, is also opening its services sector wider. A citywide data-export negative list now covers nine sectors, including medical devices, and opening-up pilots are underway in value-added telecommunications and biotechnology areas, said Tang, the city's vice-mayor. zhangchenxu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China unveils plan to expedite major projects
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
China unveils plan to expedite major projects Policymakers intensify efforts to expand effective investment, stimulate demand China is accelerating the construction of major State-backed projects and building a pipeline for 2027, as policymakers intensify efforts to expand effective investment, stimulate domestic demand and channel spending toward strategic infrastructure and technology. The National Development and Reform Commission, the country's top economic regulator, said on Friday it is urging local authorities to coordinate physical construction with supportive institutional reforms under the "two priorities" initiative, which focuses on implementing major national strategies and building the nation's security capacity in key areas, while ensuring the prudent and efficient use of funds. The aim is to expedite project delivery and generate tangible "physical workload" on the ground as quickly as possible, Li Chao, deputy director of the NDRC's policy research office, told a news conference in Beijing. The NDRC is stepping up planning for a 2027 project pipeline, Li added. The push comes as China actively transitions toward higher-quality growth, channeling capital into advanced manufacturing, new infrastructure and green transitions while reducing reliance on traditional real estate-driven expansion. The NDRC said it is coordinating with relevant departments to accelerate the deployment of new policy-based financial instruments and expand support for private investment and optimize financing mechanisms for the "six networks" initiative. The network program covers water, power, computing, next-generation communications, urban pipelines and logistics. Separately, S&P Global Ratings affirmed China's sovereign credit ratings at "A+/A-1" with a stable outlook on Friday. The agency said proactive fiscal support should help keep growth above 4 percent over the next one to two years, as the economy steadily navigates ongoing property adjustments. Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, said the heightened policy focus on the "six networks" indicates that key strategic projects are swiftly moving from the drawing board to the construction phase. "As preparatory work concludes and construction picks up pace, infrastructure investment is poised to accelerate markedly in the second half of the year, providing solid support for overall fixed-asset investment," Luo said. Xiong Yuan, chief economist at Guosheng Securities, said the "two priorities" initiative and network infrastructure will systematically address the shortage of high-return, bankable projects at the local level, though he noted that the structural transition toward emerging industries will be a steady, compounding process. Su Jian, director of Peking University's National Center for Economic Research, said the projects under the "two priorities" initiative carry strategic, nationwide significance. By combining physical construction with institutional and market reforms, such initiatives provide immediate support to macroeconomic stability while laying a durable foundation for technological innovation, future industries and new quality productive forces. The tangible benefits of targeted investment are already visible in strategic sectors such as semiconductors. NDRC data showed that investment in integrated circuit manufacturing in the first seven months of the year rose 11.5 percent year-on-year. Among listed companies in the sector that had disclosed interim results by Thursday, aggregate revenue rose 12.8 percent year-on-year and net profit increased 99 percent, while research and development spending increased 13.4 percent, according to the NDRC. Roger Sheng, vice-president at US research firm Gartner, said China is seeking a more flexible policy framework to mobilize resources in the integrated circuit sector while avoiding wasteful investment. Chinese companies are narrowing the technological gap with global leaders, Sheng said, though bottlenecks remained in areas including lithography equipment. Contact the writers at lijing2009@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Lotus festivals reveal imperial charm
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
For many Beijingers, the lotus is not just a flower in a park; it is a part of summer. Families plant lotus tubs in the courtyards of old homes, while the flower's leaves and seeds are used to enhance the nourishing quotient of homemade porridge. This year, however, the city's lotus season is bigger than the courtyards. Thirteen parks, including Beihai Park, the Summer Palace and Yuanmingyuan Ruins Park, are hosting lotus festivals, which lean into the flower's imperial history. Visitors can watch performances in ancient style, take part in ceremonies built around lotus-scented teas, join stamp-collection activities and try royal-themed drinks. The bloom is drawing foreign photographers and vloggers in droves. Canadian photographer Madelyn Arnold shared her photos on the Beijing municipal government's website, in the "Beijing Through Foreigners' Lens" section. "I was fully immersed in the beauty of the blooming lotus flowers and the good fortune they represent," Arnold wrote. Scottish photographer Bruce Connolly, who has lived in China for 39 years, posted an image of lotuses blooming against the backdrop of white clouds over Shichahai on his WeChat Moments and LinkedIn account. Shichahai is a well-preserved traditional residential area in Beijing's Xicheng district, and one of the busiest tourist spots in the city. "Walking along the waterway on the Central Axis toward Yinding Bridge, then along Qianhai, the lotus lane is unforgettable, especially when photographing at sunset," Connolly said. At Beihai Park, one of China's earliest and best-preserved imperial gardens, lotus flowers have bloomed for more than 800 years. Zhang Meng, a seasoned docent there, said that locals treat lotus viewing as a shared ritual. "For typical Beijingers, visiting Beihai to appreciate lotus flowers in the cool summer or breezy early autumn is a shared passion," she said. In the early 2000s, the park introduced more than 3,000 lotus plants, some grown from seeds that had been sent to space as part of a national scientific project. Today, lotus-themed souvenirs and lotus-flavored drinks at the park's cafes have become hugely popular. Serbian vlogger Katarina Stojanovic, a graduate from Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, pays attention to how the plant is used. She noted that Empress Dowager Cixi of the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) enjoyed summer drinks made with lotus seeds, which are known for their medicinal value. Stojanovic tried a lotus-flavored drink at the Summer Palace. "It was so refreshing and cooling," she said. "The lotus is not just for appreciation; it serves both medicinal and culinary purposes. Lotus seeds nourish the heart, calm the mind and strengthen the spleen." For Connolly, the Scottish photographer, the appeal is simple. "Although it's been 39 years since I first set out to discover and photograph Beijing, the passion still remains within me," he said. "Walking in the city, there is always something fascinating to capture through the lens."

item.title: Local for local: a paradigm shift for business
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
Local for local: a paradigm shift for business German companies compete, innovate, and develop in China to sharpen their global competitiveness. Germany's economy has returned to growth in 2026, but whether Europe's largest economy has finally left years of stagnation behind remains far from certain. According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's real GDP expanded by 0.4 percent quarter-on-quarter in the first three months of the year and by another 0.2 percent in the second quarter. While the figures point to a tentative recovery after years of economic weakness, a combination of domestic constraints and external shocks continues to cast a shadow over the outlook for the second half of the year. The situation is being worsened by climate change, with heat and drought sending water levels plunging on the Rhine, which is one of Europe's most important commercial waterways. Near Cologne, the receding water levels that have disrupted inland shipping have been so severe they exposed a 500-kilogram unexploded United States World War II bomb. Germany's energy-intensive industries are facing another squeeze as conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and raw material costs. The Leibniz Institute for Economic Research at the University of Munich (ifo Institute) has estimated that the energy shock alone could shave about 0.4 percentage points off German economic growth this year, while exports to the US fell 14.2 percent month-on-month in June with uncertainty created by US tariff and trade policies. Eberhard J. Trempel, director-general of the German Global Trade Forum Berlin, has argued that Germany's competitiveness is being weighed down by high energy and raw material costs, heavy tax and social-security burdens, high labor costs, slow approval procedures, and a shortage of skilled workers. Against this backdrop, German businesses are searching more urgently for new sources of growth. Strategy by increments There has been no single declaration that German industry has found a new answer to its problems at home. Instead, the direction becomes visible through a series of major corporate decisions made in different sectors for different reasons. On March 26, German chemical giant BASF officially inaugurated its newly built Verbund site in Zhanjiang city, Guangdong province, a sprawling industrial complex covering around 4 square kilometers and representing an investment of 8.7 billion euros ($10.15 billion). The investment is particularly striking because it comes as Germany's chemical industry has struggled with high energy costs, subdued demand, and concerns about industrial competitiveness at home. "Zhanjiang shows what the future of chemistry looks like: efficient, digital, and sustainable by design," BASF CEO Markus Kamieth said at the inauguration. The project was completed on schedule and below its original budget, and the site is powered entirely by renewable electricity, and most of what it produces will be sold directly to customers in China under BASF's "local-for-local" strategy. "This investment shows confidence in the world's largest chemical market in the long run," Kamieth said. The decision reflects a broader shift in how some German companies think about China as its largest trading partner. Rather than manufacturing primarily in Germany and shipping products eastward, they are increasingly putting production, research and development closer to Chinese customers. Shi Shiwei, director of the Research Center for Europe at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said: "German companies are increasingly embracing a local-for-local strategy, not only selling in China but also conducting research and development, manufacturing, and innovation there. Staying competitive in China can, in turn, strengthen their competitiveness globally." Trempel said China remains an "indispensable market" for key German industries including machinery, automobiles, chemicals and electrical engineering. Its scale can help German companies lower costs and maintain global competitiveness, while Chinese ecosystems in electric mobility, batteries, renewable energy and digital infrastructure also offer opportunities for technological cooperation. The same logic extends beyond traditional heavy industry. For Bayer, another German industrial heavyweight, China is increasingly important, not simply because of the size of its pharmaceutical market, but because of what is being invented there. The company has been expanding an innovation network that links Chinese biotech companies, universities, and research institutions with Bayer's global pharmaceutical development system. In late May, Bayer held an R&D Open Day at the Beijing center, describing China as an integral part of its pharmaceutical research strategy. Stefan Oelrich, a member of the board of management of Bayer AG and head of its Pharmaceuticals Division, told China Daily that China has "one of the most dynamic innovation systems in the pharmaceuticals industry". "China's pharmaceuticals market is, and will remain, a strategic priority for Bayer, and we are continuing to deepen our innovation footprint there," Oelrich said. The shift in language is significant. Bayer no longer describes China only as a destination for medicines developed elsewhere. "Innovation capabilities in China are a strategic pillar of Bayer's global innovation strategy," Oelrich said. "We see China not only as one of our most important markets, but increasingly as an innovation engine feeding directly into our global pipeline." China's biotech industry, academic institutions, clinical capabilities, and digital infrastructure would therefore remain central to Bayer's long-term strategy, he said. "If we want to remain at the forefront of our industry, we need to be where innovation happens. China is clearly one of those places, and an increasingly important one." A similar message has come from Bosch. The German engineering and technology group established the Bosch Robotics Center China in January, focusing on embodied artificial intelligence and humanoid robotics. The company hopes to combine its own expertise in sensors, software, drives and industrial automation with China's manufacturing capacity, supply chains, industrial data and rapidly developing robotics ecosystem. "China is a source of highly qualified talent and strong innovative capacity," then Bosch chairman Stefan Hartung told China Daily at the company's annual media day in April this year. "The Chinese market has requirements unlike those in almost any other market, and this leads to enormous customer focus, great speed, and intense competition." Adapting to circumstances Despite operating in different industries, BASF, Bayer, and Bosch have each made moves that have culminated in a turn toward China. For some of Germany's biggest industrial companies, the country is evolving from primarily a sales market into a place where products are manufactured, technologies developed and new business models tested. The attraction is easy to understand. China, the world's second-largest economy, expanded by 5 percent in 2025. With its vast consumer market, complete manufacturing ecosystem and rapidly developing innovation landscape, the country remains difficult for German industry to ignore despite growing competition and geopolitical uncertainties. Behind the trust is the unusually broad and dense industrial ecosystem of China, which brings together suppliers of sensors, electronics, batteries, motors, precision components and production equipment with software developers and engineering talent, thus creating convenience and lowering costs. In a report published last year, Reuters cited a source as saying that iPhone manufacturing costs in India remained 5 to 8 percent higher than in China, with the gap reaching as much as 10 percent in some cases. Semiconductor industry analyst Chen Jing said the experience-curve concept developed by Bruce Henderson at Boston Consulting Group in the 1960s holds that production costs fall by 10 to 15 percent each time cumulative industrial output doubles. " That rule applies accurately today to China, because other economies cannot match its ability to spread costs across such enormous production volumes, making it highly attractive to investors from major European economies." Pragmatic new ties But the economic relationship is not becoming simpler. German exports to China fell by more than 12 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to less than 37 billion euros, even as German exports overall rose 3.7 percent. Chinese companies, meanwhile, have become challengers in sectors once regarded as German industrial strongholds. Thomas Konig, senior China affairs expert at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry, or DIHK, sees less contradiction in those trends than the headline numbers might suggest. "Despite geopolitical headwinds, China remains a vital market," Konig told China Daily. "Over 50 percent of German companies operating here state that the Chinese market is of central importance to their global competitiveness." The era in which foreign companies could count on rapid, double-digit Chinese growth may have passed, he said, but that does not make China less relevant. Instead, it is changing the nature of the relationship. "The overall outlook is one of cautious optimism. The era of breakneck, double-digit growth may be over, but a new chapter is beginning," Konig said. German companies' role in China is changing, Konig pointed out, saying: "German companies are no longer just selling to China; they are innovating in and with China to strengthen their competitiveness here and globally." For decades, one of the simplest descriptions of Sino-German economic relations was that Germany sold machinery, automobiles, chemicals and other sophisticated industrial products to a rapidly industrializing China, said Jian Junbo, a professor and the director of Center for China-Europe Relations, Fudan University. Shi Shiwei echoed this. "The China-Germany economic relationship was traditionally seen as highly complementary, with China providing a vast market and manufacturing capacity while Germany supplied sophisticated products in sectors such as automobiles, machinery and chemicals," Shi said. "But as Chinese companies become increasingly competitive in electric vehicles, machinery, green technologies and other fields, the relationship is evolving into one characterized by complementarity, competition and cooperation at the same time." The fact that China is not only a consumer but also a producer, technology developer, and increasingly powerful challenger is described by Trempel as a "paradigm shift" for German business: from "Made in Germany for China" toward "local for local". German companies are increasingly conducting research and development in China rather than merely adapting products developed in Germany. Shorter development cycles — particularly in electric vehicles, batteries, software, and AI — are encouraging them to use Chinese supplier ecosystems and digital platforms, he said. At the same time, the flow of knowledge is becoming more two-way. Innovations developed under China's intense competition and cost pressure can increasingly feed back into products for European and global markets. Konig pointed to smart manufacturing, medical technology, renewable energy and the circular economy as areas offering considerable scope for deeper cooperation. "From electric mobility to industrial efficiency, from medical care to smart AI programs, there remains substantial room for German and Chinese companies to work together," he said. That assessment closely resembles what German executives themselves are doing, but none of the experts interviewed suggested ignoring the difficulties facing China-Germany economic relations. Konig said German companies continue to seek greater market access and better treatment, more transparent regulatory processes and reliable intellectual-property protection. Export controls on rare earths are another immediate concern. "German companies need to continue adapting to the demands of the Chinese market to remain competitive," he said. "The governments of both sides must help to set guardrails for this cooperation and to protect the interests of their respective companies." Trempel likewise argued that closer cooperation comes with risks ranging from unequal market access to geopolitical tensions and competitive pressure. But he rejected the idea that risk reduction should become an argument for dismantling economic ties. Risk assessment, he said, has always been part of business. Companies routinely decide where risks are acceptable and where they are not. For Germany, he argued, the more sustainable approach is to protect genuinely critical technologies and infrastructure while continuing cooperation in areas where the two sides have common interests. "A pragmatic deepening of cooperation can serve as a catalyst for recovery, provided it is accompanied by fair framework conditions," Trempel said. For Konig, the same pragmatism is visible in companies' long-term commitment to China. "From a German business perspective, our commitment to this market is pragmatic, strategic, and long-term," he said. zhangzhouxiang@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Live: Rescuers struggle to reopen Gyirong Port route
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang HONG KONG -- John Lee Ka-chiu, chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, said on Saturday that HK$50 million ($6.37 million) has been earmarked from the Disaster Relief Fund following a mudslide that hit the Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region. In a post on social media, Lee expressed deep sadness over the disaster, mourning the victims and extending his sincere sympathies to those affected and the bereaved families. Lee hoped that the rescue operations would proceed safely and smoothly, and that the affected residents would receive timely support to overcome the hardships. He added that the Disaster Relief Fund Advisory Committee will process funding applications expeditiously. "Is anyone there?" In Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, rescue workers are calling out for signs of life, their voices echoing around the mudslide-devastated valleys. Days after a mudslide tore through Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, search and rescue teams are racing against difficult and hazardous terrain to comb through core areas, maintaining continuous and uninterrupted operations. After a mudslide struck Gyirong border port, Shigatse, Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, engineering crews made robust efforts to reinforce power facilities, ensuring uninterrupted telecommunication connections for rescue operations. Comprehensive efforts are in motion to reestablish road connectivity to Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, following a devastating mudslide originating in Nepal. The calamity has inflicted severe damage on the G216 highway, the main access route to the port, creating significant obstacles for rescue and relief operations. Zhu Feng, chief engineer at China Anneng Construction Group's Chengdu rescue base, said on Saturday that they deployed 60 technicians and 28 pieces of heavy equipment, including excavators and loaders, to the affected area on the G216 highway leading to the port. Following a disaster risk assessment and monitoring of surrounding hazards, members from the group, a State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, commenced operations to clear a 2-kilometer damaged section near the port, with the goal of facilitating the efficient implementation of subsequent rescue and disposal efforts, Zhu added. On Aug 29, a massive mudslide cut off Highway G216 near Gyirong Port, Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. To secure this vital rescue passage, the State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng Construction Group has deployed 60 specialists and 28 sets of machinery to reopen the roughly 2-kilometer road, with the company’s teams assessing and monitoring potential risks and hazards. Efforts to reinforce power and base station infrastructure are advancing to ensure uninterrupted communication for rescue operations following a severe mudslide at a border port in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. On Saturday morning, engineering crews shored up power facilities, guaranteeing uninterrupted telecommunications connections for relief operations. "Our goal is to ensure that communications keep pace with road clearance, rolling out power facilities and network coverage simultaneously, so that the telecommunications network truly becomes a lifeline for rescue and relief operations," said Kelsang Norbu, manager of the operations and maintenance department for China Tower's Xizang branch, one of the world's largest telecommunications tower infrastructure service providers. He told China Daily that the immediate priority on Saturday was strengthening auxiliary infrastructure, particularly boosting power supply to facilitate broader network coverage. The team working on reinforcing communication links include members from China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom. Days after a mudslide tore through Gyirong Port, Xizang autonomous region, search and rescue teams are racing against difficult and hazardous terrain to comb through core areas, maintaining continuous and uninterrupted operations. On Saturday morning, the land search and rescue team from the Sichuan Fire and Rescue Corps under the China Rescue Team, dispatched by the Ministry of Emergency Management and the National Fire and Rescue Administration, continued to search through debris at the mudslide site near Gyirong Port. LHASA -- Seven people had been killed, and 554 others remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued as of 1 am on Saturday after a mudslide struck the Gyirong Port along the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, according to the region's emergency management department. A total of 2,141 rescue workers and 86 specialists from natural resources and other relevant fields have been deployed to the disaster area. With specialized equipment, they have stepped up inspections for geological hazards across surrounding slopes, roads and other critical zones. A five-person monitoring post has been set up to keep the barrier lake under constant observation and guard against potential secondary disasters. In addition, 1.02 kilometers of road have been cleared and reopened to traffic. The mudslide, which occurred on the Nepalese side, struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong county of Xizang on Wednesday morning. Rescue and road-clearing operations are advancing into the heart of mudslide-stricken Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, where vehicles lie twisted and mangled by the force of the disaster. Since Saturday morning, teams from the Ministry of Emergency Management and National Fire and Rescue Administration have been actively working in the disaster-stricken areas near the Gyirong border port. As excavators assist in the effort, team members are conducting thorough inspections, carefully navigating the region's challenging terrain. Workers from China Anneng Construction Group, a State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise, told China Daily that they are approximately 1.8 to 2 kilometers from the port, an area severely affected by the massive mudslide that struck Nepal on Wednesday, resulting in significant casualties. Rescue teams are continuing to push toward the core mudslide-hit area in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, through forested mountains and murky waters, as damaged roads, disrupted utilities, frequent rainfall and an overflowing barrier lake continue to complicate the dogged search for missing people. Around 4:30 pm on Friday, six members from the first response team of the Xizang fire and rescue brigade and 15 members — along with one search-and-rescue dog — from the first response team of the Sichuan fire and rescue brigade reached the Gyirong border port, which bore the maximum brunt of the deadly mudslide on the Chinese side. These were the first professional rescue teams to reach the core area, Xinhua News Agency reported. Even as damaged roads, disabled communication systems and snapped power supplies hindered rescue and relief efforts a day after the disaster, workers remained determined to achieve results. They cleared and repaired overnight a nearly 1-kilometer stretch of a 2.8-km approach road to the border gate. Jigme Dorje, Party chief of the Nyalam maintenance section of the Shigatse highway development center, said eight machines — including four excavators and four loaders — and more than 20 workers were clearing and repairing the road. Local volunteers and enterprises are also supporting their efforts, he added. Xia Mingyong, from the Lhasa fire and rescue mobile detachment, said the team's rescuers were advancing by land and water. "On land, we are mainly moving toward the border port on foot. In water, we are using rubber boats to reach the severely affected port area," he said. On Friday, a barrier lake that formed upstream of Gyirong port topped 90 million cubic feet of water, up from the estimated 50-70 million cubic feet recorded on Thursday, raising the risk of secondary disasters, agencies reported. The overflow sparked panic and warnings from Nepalese authorities, leading to rescue operations being suspended in Nepal for about three hours. The risk of the lake bursting also prompted rescue personnel and vehicles on the Chinese side to be on standby in a safe area, China Central Television reported. Both sides resumed rescue operations after the threat eased. "By noon, as the risk posed by the upstream barrier lake was deemed manageable, rescue operations for the Gyirong mudslide disaster quickly resumed and were stepped up," CCTV said. According to a news release by Chinese authorities, a total of 2,096 rescuers, including firefighters, police personnel and medical workers, have been deployed in the county. More than 300 vehicles, drones and two satellite communications vehicles are being used for rescue, evacuation guidance, reconnaissance and frontline communications. Furthermore, 32 experts are conducting on-site surveys of barrier lakes to support decision-making, while a five-member observation post has been set up to monitor the two lakes in real time and prevent secondary disasters. Fire and rescue teams have set up three task groups to reach the hardest-hit area by rubber boats and by scaling mountains on foot, and for using drones for reconnaissance and supply deliveries. Small teams mobilized in advance are also monitoring the core disaster area and the barrier lake with drones and binoculars. Local authorities said 499 affected residents have already been resettled and 555 stranded tourists evacuated. Shigatse has allocated more than 15,000 relief items, with additional rescue supplies to be allocated based on actual need. Wednesday's disaster was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal. The ice-and-rock collapse evolved into a massive debris flow and then into a forceful mudslide, destroying everything in its path, including the border port. Meteorological authorities have forecast frequent rainfall through Sunday and warned of possible secondary disasters. Contact the writers at yangzekun@chinadaily.com.cn Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, chaired a Party leadership meeting on Friday to deliberate and make arrangements to strengthen rescue and relief efforts in the Xizang autonomous region, where the Gyirong land port along the China-Nepal border and its surrounding areas were hit by a catastrophic mudslide on Wednesday morning. At the start of the meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Xi, who is also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, and other leaders observed a moment of silence to mourn the victims of the disaster. As of press time on Friday, five people were confirmed dead and more than 500 still missing in Gyirong county in Xizang's Shigatse. Nepal has reported 579 deaths, while more than 1,900 people are missing there. On Friday, Xi sent a message of condolence to Nepal's President Ram Chandra Poudel over the mudslide, which was triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse. On behalf of the Chinese government and people, Xi expressed deep condolences for the deceased and offered sincere sympathies to the bereaved families, the injured and the people in the disaster-stricken areas. During the Political Bureau meeting, it was noted that emergency rescue operations in Gyirong county in Xizang's Shigatse have so far been carried out in a swift, orderly and well-coordinated manner under the strong leadership of the CPC Central Committee, with comprehensive efforts underway for the resettlement of affected people and for proper handling of the aftermath. The disaster occurred in a severely cold plateau region with steep valleys, variable weather and many surrounding glaciers and glacial lakes, and potential geological hazards are posing significant challenges to emergency rescue operations, the meeting said. It was emphasized that all relevant authorities and departments should take resolute and effective measures for rescue-related work, search and rescue plans should be formulated in a scientific manner, and every effort should be made to search for and rescue all missing Chinese and foreign nationals. The Party leadership also underlined the need to strengthen multi-department joint consultations, enhance monitoring and early-warning systems, and closely track the stability of the barrier lake and surrounding mountains to effectively prevent secondary disasters. It is essential to reinforce the management of on-site personnel to ensure safety throughout the rescue process, the meeting said, urging proper arrangements for the affected people and meticulous attention to post-disaster relief and support. China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit areas in neighboring Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation, the Party leadership decided. The importance of balancing development and security, preparing for the extreme and worst-case scenarios, and bearing a strong sense of political responsibility and constant vigilance to ensure security and stability in all aspects of work was emphasized at the meeting. Meanwhile, Xi, in his condolence message to Poudel, noted that China and Nepal are connected by mountains and rivers and share a common destiny. China is willing to actively aid Nepal in its rescue efforts and provide support and assistance to the best of its capability, he said. Xi expressed his belief that the people of both countries will be able to work together to prevail over the disaster and rebuild their homes as soon as possible. Premier Li Qiang also sent a message of condolence to Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah. Entrusted by Xi, the Chinese premier traveled to Gyirong county on Thursday to guide rescue and emergency response efforts. While assessing the ground situation and meeting with rescue teams, Li emphasized the need to put the people and their lives above all else and spare no effort in carrying out rescue operations and emergency response work. He said that as long as there is a glimmer of hope, every effort should be made to search for and rescue still those missing. Li later visited temporary shelters for affected residents and conveyed President Xi's concern and care to them. The premier emphasized the need to continue dispatching and transporting disaster-relief supplies and ensure the basic living needs of evacuated and relocated residents. Li heard reports from local authorities and relevant departments about the disaster, and discussed further efforts in rescue and emergency response measures. He highlighted the need to coordinate the deployment of rescue forces and equipment, strengthen on-site unified command and thoroughly ascertain the status of missing persons to conduct effective rescues. Transparency in the release of information regarding the disaster and rescue operations is crucial, he added. caodesheng@chinadaily.com.cn There is something especially revealing about politicians who seek to exploit a natural disaster for political gain. After the catastrophic landslide and flash flood that struck Nepal and China's Xizang autonomous region this week, causing heavy casualties, some secessionist-minded officials of Democratic Progressive Party authorities of China's Taiwan region, including Hsiao Bi-khim and Wu Chao-hsieh sought to capitalize on it. In their so-called "condolences", they framed the disaster as being at the "Tibet-Nepal border", studiously avoiding any mention of the fact that Xizang is part of China. The wording may look "innocuous" to the casual reader. But it is anything but innocuous. For officials associated with a party whose political project is deeply entangled with separatist thinking, the omission is the message. What came next was even more grotesque: A pro-DPP media outlet reportedly claimed that Nepal's disaster relief efforts were delayed because "the mainland gave no early warning". Really? Scientific evidence points to a cascading geophysical disaster that began on the Nepalese side. A high-altitude glacier collapse sent ice and rock down the mountain, picking up huge quantities of loose debris and eventually generating a devastating mudslide that struck Gyirong Port in Xizang. Experts have emphasized how little reaction time was available. The flow traveled at roughly 50 meters per second, covering nearly 14 miles in just 6 minutes and 50 seconds, leaving virtually no time to react. The United States Geological Survey later confirmed there was no earthquake involved and the event was "a glacial collapse and debris flow" that "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream". Yet somehow a natural catastrophe becomes, in the pro-DPP media outlet's telling, another indictment of Beijing. Scientists have warned that rising temperatures are destabilizing glaciers, permafrost and high-altitude slopes, increasing the risk of cascading hazards in the Himalayas. The climate crisis is a global challenge, not a convenient accusation to be hurled across the Taiwan Strait. This is what happens when ideology overrides compassion. Beijing's response to the disaster was swift. Authorities activated emergency responses, mobilized the military, firefighting and specialist rescue teams, deployed helicopters, drones and heavy equipment, and coordinated with Nepal on search-and-rescue operations. Beijing also said it was prepared to provide emergency assistance according to Kathmandu's needs. Many foreign leaders and international organization chiefs, including UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, have expressed grief over the loss of life in both Nepal and China, while the UN said humanitarian partners were supporting relief operations in the two countries. The Taiwan secessionists' response is to turn a landslide into a despicable political spectacle. The UN's disaster-risk chief later described the catastrophe as a reminder of the "transboundary nature" of disaster risks and the fragility of mountain ecosystems. Hsiao and Wu may believe that carefully deleting the word "China" makes a political point. It does. It tells grieving families that even in death, tragedy serves ideology for the secessionists of the DPP authorities. The pro-DPP media outlet, with its ugly performance, has also exposed its true colors as a political tool of the DPP authorities. One that is always ready to stoop to new lows in spreading fake news. The DPP authorities' brazen attempt to smuggle their separatist agenda into a disaster zone and shamelessly pretend it is compassion has been denounced by people on both sides of the Strait. The DPP's politicization of this tragedy runs counter to the true feelings of compatriots on the island. While firmly opposing the DPP authorities' separatist opportunism, it should be acknowledged that people on both sides of the Strait have always stood together in times of disaster. A glacier collapsed. Rivers surged. Mud buried lives. But for some Taiwan secessionists that is free publicity for their cause, not a tragedy to be lamented. China's national comprehensive fire and rescue force carried out search and rescue operations near Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region on Friday. The Shigatse detachment of the People's Armed Police Force Xizang Contingent was deployed to the area near Gyirong Port for search and rescue operations on Friday. The Sichuan Fire and Rescue Brigade has deployed a forward command team to assist rescue operations in Gyirong county of Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, after a deadly mudslide on the Nepal side of the border struck the Gyirong Port area on Wednesday, causing significant casualties and leaving many missing. Immediately after the disaster, the brigade activated an emergency response and dispatched 155 personnel to the affected area, with a second team of 450 personnel on standby for rescue operations. At 9 am on Thursday, a 10-member forward command team sent by the brigade arrived at Heping Airport in Shigatse and drove directly to Gyirong town to join frontline rescuers, the brigade said. A meeting held by the brigade on Thursday morning showed that the rugged terrain, unstable slopes from previous quakes, recent persistent rainfall, and a 2,000-meter elevation drop along the rescue route posed a high risk of new barrier lakes. The meeting called for around-the-clock monitoring of rescue areas, prevention against secondary disasters to ensure the safety of rescuers, and dedicated logistics and medical support channels to support long-term rescue operations, according to the brigade. Rescue teams are using ropes to get themselves and rubber boats across torrential rapids in the Xizang autonomous region. They plan to conduct rescue operations by kayak in the mudslide-stricken Gyirong Port in Shigatse. More than 100 power repair personnel and dozens of emergency power units have been deployed to Gyirong county following the mudslide in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, State Grid Xizang Electric Power said on Friday. As of 10 am, 106 repair personnel, 13 emergency power vehicles, 52 generators, and 39 lighting units had arrived in the affected areas to support power restoration. Additional equipment has also been mobilized from other regions, including 19 lighting units, two drone-based lighting systems, and two mobile charging stations. The equipment is on standby for deployment based on conditions at the disaster sites. The company said it would continue to reinforce emergency power support and deploy additional personnel and equipment as needed to accelerate restoration work. A mudslide that began on the Nepalese side of the border on Wednesday morning hit the Gyirong Port area in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, leaving three people dead and 558 others missing as of 8 am Thursday. Rescue work is continuing. How have rescue operations progressed? Gyirong township lies on the southern slope of the Himalayas, bordering Nepal. Its steep terrain and narrow valleys have made rescue operations extremely difficult. Rescuers said mud in the core disaster area was more than 1.5 meters deep, while possible ground subsidence further slowed the movement of personnel and machinery. The mudslide also destroyed sections of the river valley. Local police warned that rising temperatures around noon could increase geological risks and urged people to leave dangerous areas quickly. Multiple rescue forces have been sent to the front line. The Ministry of Emergency Management dispatched teams to Xizang, and as of around 8 am on Thursday, the first group of 141 rescuers had arrived at Gyirong Port. A plateau-type Mi-171 helicopter had also reached the disaster area. Forces from the Xizang Military Command, armed police, fire and rescue teams, the China Search and Rescue Team and China Anneng Group - which specializes in the engineering element of rescue operations - have joined the operation. Shigatse has activated a Level I emergency response for natural disaster relief. Norbu Tsering, commander-in-chief of the disaster frontline command, deputy secretary of the Communist Party of China Shigatse Municipal Committee and acting mayor of Shigatse, said two villagers from Resuo village had been rescued as of 8 am on Thursday. What caused the disaster? Experts at the Ministry of Natural Resources said the disaster was triggered by the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. The falling ice rushed downhill at high speed, sweeping up moraine deposits and turning into a debris flow. It then entered the Donglin Zangbo River, forming a mudslide that struck Gyirong Port and continued downstream through the canyon. Guo Zhaocheng, director of the geological disaster investigation and monitoring center at the China Aero Geophysical Survey and Remote Sensing Center for Land and Resources, described it as a chain reaction from ice collapse to debris flow and then mudslide. The debris flow moved at an estimated speed of about 50 meters per second and affected an area more than 20 kilometers away. Yao Tandong of the Chinese Academy of Sciences said glacier-related disasters are becoming more frequent, wider in range and more destructive amid global warming. In this case, disaster energy moved down the valley and was amplified downstream, increasing both damage and secondary risks. Rescuers said the terrain encountered by the mudslide as it rushed downstream did little to slow or absorb its force, making its impact especially destructive when it reached Gyirong Port. They said the disaster originated in a high-altitude, complex mountainous area of Nepal, where source-area inspections are difficult and early warning signs are hard to detect. Gyirong Port is a major trade channel between China and Nepal, with concentrated personnel, buildings and business activities. Rescuers said casualty figures may be higher because the disaster occurred during daytime working hours. What challenges do rescuers face? Rescuers said the main challenges are unstable terrain, damaged roads, poor weather and disrupted communications. Local authorities said a barrier lake had formed upstream after the ice collapse, posing a threat to downstream rescue work. Mudslides were still occurring near Langdang Snow Mountain, and drones were being used to monitor the lake because of fast-flowing river water and unsafe ground conditions. Road damage has also slowed rescue access. A section about 3 kilometers from the main disaster site was damaged. On Wednesday, with roads blocked, an advance team of more than 10 police and fire rescuers used three large machines but managed to advance only about 600 meters. Rain, fading light and deep river water further complicated the operation. By Thursday morning, several local officials and front-line rescuers said the roadbed had been severely damaged, and the river remained deep and fast-flowing, adding to the difficulty of rescue work. Communications and power were cut off in the affected area. Five base stations along the route from Gyirong township to the border port were destroyed by floodwater. At around 4 pm on Thursday, communication signals were restored in Resuo village, about 3 kilometers from Gyirong Port. Meteorological authorities have forecast frequent rain in Gyirong county until Sunday, with heavy rain possible in some low-altitude southern townships, along with high temperature variation between night and day. Mountain torrents, mudslide and landslide may occur in some areas. How are affected people being aided? After the disaster, national authorities activated a Level-II emergency response for disaster relief, the second-highest in China's four-level disaster relief emergency response system, and the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Emergency Management allocated 120 million yuan ($17.85 million) in central disaster relief funds. Local governments have organized evacuations and temporary resettlement. Police involved in rescue work have moved more than 300 Gyirong residents to safety. Shigatse has allocated more than 15,000 relief items, including tents, blankets, cold-weather clothing, folding beds and daily necessities. Sixty-two temporary tents have been set up to meet basic living needs. At a temporary settlement about 20 kilometers from Gyirong Port, each tent is equipped with beds, quilts and pillows. Power support equipment, emergency lighting and charging facilities are also available. The National Health Commission is coordinating medical treatment, transfer of the injured and psychological support. Xizang has opened a 24-hour psychological assistance hotline, while hospitals, blood supply units and national emergency medical rescue teams are on standby. Meteorological departments at four levels are increasing coordination, using satellite remote sensing and weather monitoring data to identify secondary disaster risks around the mudslide-hit area. Forecasts are being updated on a rolling basis to support rescue operations. Experts warned that people should avoid valleys, river channels, low-lying areas and cliffside slopes during rainfall and remain alert to mudslide and landslide for 72 hours after rain ends. GYIRONG, Xizang -- Rescue forces have been quickly deployed to a mudslide-hit port along the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, but relief operations remain severely hampered by complex and dangerous conditions on the ground. Official figures show that a fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepalese side, swept through Gyirong Port on Wednesday morning. As of 8 am on Thursday, three people had been killed, 558 remained missing, while two local villagers had been rescued. Xinhua reporters at the scene said the mudslide had devastated the river valley below. The silt layer in the core disaster area is more than 1.5 meters deep, posing a high risk of trapping anyone caught in it. Chinese rescue teams mobilized swiftly to the remote mountainous border region. The first contingent of 141 emergency rescuers reached Gyirong Port on Thursday morning. Another 111 members of China's national search and rescue team arrived in Gyirong county by 2:28 pm Thursday. The People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command has deployed two batches of military helicopters to conduct aerial assessments, map rescue flight routes and carry out intensive searches, while also ferrying medical and rescue equipment to the affected area. Despite these efforts, rescuers on site say operations are extremely challenging due to several factors. The first is the risk of secondary disasters. The meteorological department forecasts light to moderate rain or thunderstorms across most of Gyirong county from Wednesday night to Sunday, with heavy rain in some southern low-altitude towns. These downpours could trigger flash floods, mudslides and mudslides in vulnerable areas, potentially disrupting rescue work. The county authorities have also warned that a barrier lake, formed upstream of the port by the glacier collapse, sits in an unstable geological setting and could breach, endangering rescue operations downstream. The second obstacle is damaged road infrastructure. Local authorities said a road about three kilometers from the site was destroyed by the mudslide, delaying rescue access and slowing response efforts. The third challenge is the temporary loss of contact with the disaster zone. In the immediate aftermath, communications and power supply were cut off, leaving the situation in the core area unknown for a time. By around 4 pm Thursday, communication signals were restored in a village three kilometers from the port, marking phased progress in emergency communication support, authorities said. The National Commission for Disaster Prevention, Reduction and Relief, together with the Ministry of Emergency Management (MEM), helped allocate 30,000 central relief supplies, including tents, stoves, clothing, quilts, folding beds and moisture-proof mats, to support evacuation, resettlement and relief work. The Ministry of Finance and the MEM also allocated 120 million yuan (about $17.7 million) in central natural disaster relief funds to support Xizang in carrying out emergency rescue and disaster relief operations. Governments at all levels in Xizang and relevant departments have promptly organized disaster prevention efforts and risk avoidance measures, and have properly relocated and resettled those under threat. A total of 499 villagers and construction workers have been properly accommodated. Meanwhile, 555 affected tourists were evacuated and transferred under the coordination of cultural and tourism authorities. No tourists remain stranded.

item.title: Qingdao 'city drink': Brewing coastal charm
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-28
In Qingdao, East China's Shandong province, the sea breeze carries the aroma of malt through century-old breweries, historic streets and crowds gathering at summer dusk. "Drink beer and eat clams", as the local saying goes, has long been part of everyday life in this coastal city. Start the day with a fresh brew and a refreshing spirit. Step into the Tsingtao Beer Museum to witness traditional beer-making techniques meet modern technology, and savor diverse flavors born from different brewing methods. Wander through the liyuan courtyards in Dabao Island, where Chinese and Western architectural styles blend with the city's everyday bustle. Join host Melissa on a 24-hour "city drink" journey through Qingdao and discover the romance of late summer!

item.title: Information resilience need of the hour
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-28
Former Kyrgyz ambassador: Information resilience need of the hour Share - WeChat
Artificial intelligence is making disinformation appear increasingly convincing. Text, images and videos can now be harder than ever to distinguish from the real thing. What does this mean for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, which brings together 10 member states representing more than 3 billion people? Kairat Osmonaliev, former ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary of the Kyrgyz Republic to the Republic of Azerbaijan and concurrently to Georgia, shared his answer in an interview with China Daily's Global Lens: the key is not to establish a common mechanism for controlling information, but to build a system of information resilience among member states, thereby safeguarding the information security of the internet.
